title: Amanda Nunes retired as the GOAT. Now she’s back for the joy of fighting
content:
When most UFC fighters retire from mixed martial arts, they ceremonially lay their gloves in the center of the cage. When Amanda Nunes announced her departure in June 2023, she left two belts there as well.

Nunes, now 38, is the most decorated woman in MMA history. Her 2023 win over Irene Aldana marked her eighth title defense, six times at bantamweight and twice at featherweight. Nunes is the only fighter in UFC history, male or female, to defend belts in two divisions while holding both titles simultaneously.

By the time she retired, she accomplished every feat a fighting career could offer.

So why come back? Why return against the dominant champion Kayla Harrison, whom Nunes called the second-greatest women’s fighter ever? Why risk a new blemish on a sterling career?

Speaking 10 days before her comeback bout at UFC 334, Nunes couldn’t stop smiling as she answered.

“I’m lucky right now. I’m in a good position because I’m gonna have fun with this fight,” she told The Athletic. “I’m going to have so much fun because I’ve had so much fun through my camp, the whole camp.”

She’s returning to the sport with a mindset she never had during her reign of domination in multiple divisions. She described those years as being “under pressure constantly.”

“And now going through this, I’m happy!” she said with a giddy laugh. “This is exactly how I wanted to feel back then, but I’m feeling it now.”

That constant pressure fueled Nunes to the top of the sport and crafted a more satisfying career arc, which could have been a more difficult path after she lost her third UFC fight.

Nunes’ career was not one of perfection, but one of triumph. She was an underdog when she first won gold, choking out Meisha Tate at UFC 200. She was an underdog again when she dominated Ronda Rousey when Rousey was at the top of her stardom, a brutal changing of the guard that needed only 48 seconds to play out.

When the legendary Cris Cyborg made her UFC arrival and threatened Nunes’ supremacy in the newly created women’s featherweight division, Nunes went up in weight to meet the call and needed only 51 seconds to dismantle Cyborg.

Her air of invincibility was zapped when Julianna Peña stunned the world to take Nunes’ bantamweight belt in 2021. Then Nunes proved herself as a challenger once again, reclaiming her gold eight months later.

By the time she defeated Aldana, there were no more mountains to climb, but that pressure amid the mundanity of dominance drained Nunes. So she took a break.

She said she’s back in the headspace she needs.

“I have the same feeling as when I fought Ronda Rousey, the same feeling when I fought Cyborg,” she said. “I’m happy. … This is the level of mindset that I like to feel. Everything is connecting from my mind, my soul, my body. I’m ready to go.”

But unlike some of Nunes’ opponents in recent years, Harrison is far from overmatched. A two-time Olympic gold medal judoka, Harrison has steamrolled her first three UFC opponents since joining the promotion in 2024, with the same grappling flair as Rousey, the first Olympian judoka to win a UFC title.

Years earlier, Harrison trained with Nunes herself at American Top Team, when Nunes was UFC champion and Harrison was transitioning from judo into MMA, competing in the PFL promotion.

Their relationship soured when Harrison made it clear she was coming for Nunes’ UFC supremacy.

Harrison won UFC gold in Nunes’ absence, dismantling Peña to win the bantamweight title in June 2025. The former teammates’ collision course was confirmed minutes after Harrison’s hand was raised, when Nunes entered the cage to face off with the new champion of her old stomping grounds.

On why Harrison’s winning gold drew Nunes back to the UFC, and plenty more, here’s more from the returning champion.

Note: Questions and answers edited lightly for length and clarity.

What was it about Harrison specifically that got you most excited for this comeback?

She’s holding my belt. This is the only thing. That is my belt. She’s the champion right now, and the thing that’s driving forward is to put my hands on my belt again.

Where do you rank Harrison among all-time women’s fighters?

I put her in second. She’s a champion, and I respect her as second place. And I feel like she’s learned a lot and she’s evolved a lot.

What did it feel like to relinquish ownership of the divisions you dominated when you retired?

Honestly, when I retired, I was in peace. I needed a rest. I needed a rest, a vacation to be able to enjoy all my accomplishments from outside. And I just wanted to see excitement in the division. It was very hard for me to see those girls want (to become champion) so bad, like I did back then.

What was it like to see other women win those titles in your absence?

I feel like right now (the intensity) is missing. I don’t see these girls want it so bad like I did back in the day. Those girls like Meisha (Tate), like Holly (Holm), like Ronda (Rousey) and Cyborg, we were on a mission. We wanted this so bad. We wanted to make women’s MMA big. We did everything to make this division great. So to see it slow down now is a little hard.

Where do you think you’ll have an advantage over Harrison in the cage?

I think my timing is going to play very well against her in striking, wrestling, and in jujitsu. I feel like my timing is going to be the key to solving it, and then doing whatever I want in this fight.

How do you envision you’ll hold up against her wrestling?

We’re gonna scramble. It’s not a secret (what Harrison’s gameplan is). It’s not gonna be easy to take me down. I’m gonna scramble, and she knows that. She knows, she knows. It’s one thing when you train with somebody; it’s another thing when you fight in the UFC cage. When you have all the adrenaline and all the things that come with it, I’m used to this.

I’m going to leave everything in there. Blood, sweat, whatever, I’m going to take my belt. There’s nothing she can do that I’m not going to capitalize on and finish the fight.

You’ve said this isn’t a retirement fight and you plan on defending the belt if you win it. What went into that decision?

When you become a champion, you got to defend the belt. And then we’re gonna defend as much as possible because this is my last shot.

I’m still young. I’m 38. I can go even further into my 40s if I want because my body feels amazing.
